entry.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: New Algorithms for Shortest Vector and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
entry.summary: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the 2ⁿ/2 Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper presents classical randomized algorithms that break the 2^{n/2} barrier for discrete Gaussian sampling and the Shortest Vector Problem in lattices. It introduces Gaussian difference dynamics, a framework that tracks expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. The approach uses thin spherical shells and a double rejection technique to control the distribution of batch samples. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce Gaussian difference dynamics and report new exponents breaking the 2^{n/2} barrier for SVP and discrete Gaussian sampling.

entry.title: Quantum time-space tradeoffs for short Merkle-Damgård collisions
entry.summary: Quantum Time-Space Tradeoffs for Short Merkle-Damgård Collisions IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies how much time and quantum memory an attacker needs to find short collisions in Merkle-Damgård hashing, under a quantum auxiliary-input random-oracle model. It introduces a structure-sensitive compressed-oracle analysis that yields tighter bounds, including a tight characterization for two-block collisions even against arbitrary quantum advice. The authors also propose the ST²B conjecture for the correct constant-success tradeoff. ★★★★ Notable: The authors develop a structure-sensitive compressed-oracle analysis, giving a tight bound for two-block collisions and resolving an open problem.

entry.title: Short collisions show Sponge and Merkle-Damgård hash designs differ under preprocessing
entry.summary: Short Collisions Separate Sponge from Merkle-Damgård IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies short collisions in salted Merkle-Damgård and Sponge hash constructions under a query-bounded preprocessing model. With identical query budgets, the authors show Sponge admits constant-probability collisions using only three message blocks, while Merkle-Damgård adversaries with B = o(T₂) blocks succeed with probability o(1). The results show that collision length interacts differently with preprocessing in the two constructions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show Sponge and Merkle-Damgård separate under query-bounded preprocessing via short collisions, reporting a three-block Sponge attack and a matching MD upper bound.

entry.title: A statistical model for ratio-based ring oscillator PUFs
entry.summary: Ratio-Based Ring Oscillator PUF Statistical Model IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper presents a mathematically derived closed-form statistical model that describes the counter value distribution of ratio-based ring oscillator physical unclonable functions (ROPUFs). The authors validate the model's assumptions using ring oscillator measurements from 218 Xilinx Artix-7 FPGAs. The model allows theoretical quantification of response entropy and enables advanced bit derivation methods, such as Equiprobable Quantization and Two-Metric Helper Data, which achieve better reliability, randomness, and bit yield than the original counter-based derivation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a closed-form statistical model of counter distributions for ratio-based ROPUFs, enabling entropy quantification and new bit derivation methods, validated on 218 FPGAs.

entry.title: Authentication complexity of Byzantine consensus: how much initial key authentication is needed to tolerate faulty parties
entry.summary: The Authentication Complexity of Byzantine Consensus IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies how much initial authentication distributed parties need to reach Byzantine broadcast and agreement despite faulty parties. Each party's public verification key is authenticated only to a chosen subset of others, modeled by a directed authentication graph. The authors define authentication complexity as the minimum number of such bindings and give a tight graph characterization of setups that support agreement. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose authentication complexity and give a tight graph characterization of initial authentication setups supporting Byzantine agreement.

entry.title: ReWY: A Faster Way to Compute Gradients for Delta-Rule Attention Models
entry.summary: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces redundant computation in the backward pass of delta-rule linear attention models such as DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2. The method preserves the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic without changing the architecture or training objective. The authors implement the reduced computation graph on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs and report speedups in low-level backward computation relative to reference implementations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce seven local WY matrix products to three by eliminating auxiliary adjoints in chunkwise backward passes, reporting 1.09–2.89× speedups on H100, H200, and Ascend 950DT.

entry.title: Optimal four-dimensional lattice quantizer and Voronoi-facet-based bounds
entry.summary: Optimality of the D₄ lattice quantizer arXiv · Oct 26, 2026The paper proves that the root lattice D4 is the unique four-dimensional lattice, up to similarity, that minimizes the normalized second moment. The computer-assisted proof combines classification of secondary cones, integration over Voronoi cells, and weighted sums of squares. In dimensions two and higher, comparison with circular cones yields a lower bound depending on the number of Voronoi facets, improving the sphere bound and recovering the hexagonal value in dimension two. The authors also prove Ajjanagadde's circular-cone concavity conjecture and derive the lattice case of his conjectured quantization bound. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove D4 uniquely minimizes the normalized second moment among four-dimensional lattices, via a computer-assisted proof and a new facet-based bound.

entry.title: Secret sharing without extractable randomness
entry.summary: Secret Sharing Despite Non-Extractable Randomness arXiv · Oct 14, 2026This paper studies the randomness needed for two-out-of-two secret sharing. Bosley and Dodis asked in 2007 whether such schemes must also allow deterministic extraction of nearly uniform bits from the randomness source. The authors answer no: for each b≥2, they build a class of flat sources with min-entropy at least b and a perfectly correct, perfectly private scheme that splits a b-bit secret into two (b+1)-bit shares. The idea is extended to other threshold settings. ★★★★ Notable: A parity-based counterexample answers Bosley and Dodis's open question negatively for two-out-of-two secret sharing and extends the construction to two-out-of-n and r-out-of-r thresholds.

entry.summary: Seed Recycling: Explicit Codes for Mixed Synchronization Errors Matching the Leading Term of the Gilbert--Varshamov Bound arXiv · Oct 11, 2026This paper presents new explicit binary codes of length n that can correct t edits, including deletions, insertions, and substitutions, which is relevant to DNA-based storage and racetrack memories. entry.title: O'ido: Open-vocabulary speech recognition on a cheap microcontroller without a neural chip
entry.summary: Oído: Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Speech Recognition on a $5 Microcontroller without a Neural Accelerator arXiv · Oct 9, 2026This paper presents O'ido, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller without a neural accelerator. It executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model using int8 quantization and a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech, it makes fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, but is not yet real time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report open-vocabulary English recognition on a ~$5 ESP32-S3 without an accelerator, with LibriSpeech WER of 3.70%/8.23%, but runtime is 1.97x audio duration, not yet real time.

entry.title: Path-Finding and State Preparation in the Security of Invariant Quantum Money
entry.summary: Anchoring the Security of Invariant Quantum Money arXiv · Sep 30, 2026This paper examines the assumptions underlying the security of quantum money based on knots and invariant money. Existing proofs rely on additional knowledge-of-path assumptions whose relation to security is unclear. When equivalence classes are orbits of efficiently computable group actions, average-case hardness of path-finding is shown to be necessary for security. For knots, forgery reduces only to an equally hard state-preparation problem, and the authors propose a falsifiable preparation assumption equivalent to security. ★★★★ Notable: The paper proposes a state-preparation assumption in place of path-finding and argues their combination is equivalent to security.

entry.title: Simulating exotic particle statistics on a quantum processor
entry.summary: Analog quantum simulation of paraparticle statistics arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper emulates a type of paraparticle, called R-paraparticles, which are indistinguishable particles with nonlocal internal degrees of freedom. The researchers use a superconducting qubit lattice to model paraparticles that obey a generalized Pauli exclusion principle. Measurements show a 180-degree phase shift under exchange, antibunching independent of internal states, and thermal occupation matching neither Bose-Einstein nor Fermi-Dirac statistics. The results show that parastatistics can be observed on quantum simulation platforms. ★★★★ Notable: The authors emulate R-paraparticle statistics on a superconducting qubit lattice, reporting a 180-degree exchange phase and antibunching under beamsplitter interference.

entry.title: Long-range entangled critical state caused by coherent errors
entry.summary: Long-range entangled criticality from coherent errors arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper shows that coherent errors can drive the clean surface code into an extended critical regime that is long-range entangled, with a diverging Markov length. The authors establish two general results linking topology, coherent information and mixed-state entanglement, and extend local recovery constructions to locally parameterized families. They apply these results to the honeycomb surface code and relate conditional mutual information to conductance in a Majorana network model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that coherent errors induce a long-range entangled critical phase in the surface code, with general results on mixed-state entanglement.

entry.title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
entry.summary: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines why language models fail at retrieval on long inputs. Across five open models, adding neutral filler barely reduces accuracy, while statements in the evidence format that give the queried key a rival value sharply lower it. The authors find that the attention left on the evidence best tracks the loss, and they release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements. ★★★★ Notable: The authors attribute retrieval context rot to attention competition rather than length, reporting results across five open models and 126,473 trials, and releasing the probe and data.

entry.title: Same words, different actions: diagnosing text-action divergence in reasoning robot models
entry.summary: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies whether visual perturbations can change the physical actions of reasoning vision-language-action models while leaving their generated rationale word-for-word identical. The authors introduce a text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic and test it on the driving model Alpamayo and the manipulation model InstructVLA. Perturbations along this direction shift actions far more than they change text, and TNAS-guided attacks induce new collisions under unchanged rationales. The authors conclude that an unchanged rationale cannot certify a safe action, so monitors must check the predicted action directly. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show visual perturbations can change actions while the rationale stays word-for-word identical, introducing TNAS diagnostic; experiments report on driving and manipulation VLAs.

entry.title: ScrambleMark: Query-free, watermark-agnostic black-box attack that evades speech watermark detection
entry.summary: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents ScrambleMark, a black-box attack that evades speech watermark detection without any queries and without knowing the specific watermarking scheme. Rather than erasing the watermark, it disrupts the structural consistency of the embedded pattern by scrambling harmonic structure, which preserves perceptual quality. The authors report nearly 97% evasion across three commercial platforms and a 4.2/5 human rating, compared with 1.1 to 1.7 for prior attacks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose evading watermarks by scrambling harmonic structure rather than erasing it, reporting about 97% evasion on three commercial platforms.

entry.title: Evaluation Contracts and Evaluation Leverage: How Sliced Gaps Can Shift Without Model Changes
entry.summary: Evaluation Contracts and Evaluation Leverage: Sliced-Gap Readings in Structured Prediction Can Move Without Model Change arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper argues that sliced performance gaps, such as the intra-inter gap in document-level relation extraction, depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract, including scoring function, gold version, threshold, and output format. With predictions held fixed, swapping the gold standard reverses a method ordering. The authors propose an evaluation leverage framework and EvalLever, a preregistered, audited evaluation workflow. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an evaluation-leverage framework showing that frozen predictions can reverse method rankings under gold or scoring contract changes, plus an audited procedure and released workflow

entry.title: Structured priors: an algebra of component priors for prior-data fitted networks
entry.summary: Structured Priors: Towards an algebra of component priors for prior-data fitted networks arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Prior-data fitted networks are usually trained on synthetic data from one hand-built generator. This paper proposes structured priors, sets of named component priors linked by operators (mixture, convolution, amplitude scaling, local transform, projection) with proven algebraic properties, implemented in the macl2l package. A mixed prior of small components matched or beat every single component on seven of eight regression benchmarks. A pre-registered test of the model-averaging predictor failed, because the networks rarely identified the generating component. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an algebra of structured priors with proven operator laws, evaluated on eight regression benchmarks, and report a failed pre-registered test.

entry.title: Communication complexity of secure multiparty computation using a random oracle, including quantum settings
entry.summary: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the communication complexity of secure multiparty computation (MPC) in the random oracle model. It shows that for MPC with preprocessing, a random oracle cannot reduce online communication, which remains bounded below by Ω(|C|·t/(n-t)). For honest majority MPC, it proves an Ω(|C|) communication lower bound and gives a matching construction for degree-2 polynomials, including inner products, when n = O(log λ). The paper also analyzes protocols that use quantum communication. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend MPC communication lower bounds to the random oracle model, give matching constructions for degree-2 polynomials, and study quantum communication limits.

entry.title: Efficient binary codes that correct edit errors at the Gilbert-Varshamov bound
entry.summary: Making Every Edit Count: Efficient Binary Edit Correction at the Gilbert-Varshamov Bound arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper constructs binary codes that reach the classical Gilbert-Varshamov redundancy guarantee for a fixed number of edit errors. For each fixed t≥1 and sufficiently large block length n, the codes correct any combination of at most t insertions, deletions, and substitutions, with redundancy at most 2t·log₂n+O_t(1). For fixed t, construction, encoding, and decoding all run in polynomial time in n, and decoding recovers the original message. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report polynomial-time constructions attaining the Gilbert-Varshamov redundancy bound for binary codes correcting up to t combined edit errors.

entry.title: Physics-informed estimation of tensegrity prestress through cable slackening
entry.summary: Physics-Informed Identification of Tensegrity Prestress across Taut-Slack Transitions arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper formulates an inverse problem for identifying prestress, damping and axial stiffness in tensegrity structures from sparse measurements. Neural networks are trained on the equation-of-motion residual in constrained Cartesian coordinates, keeping a tension-only cable law so that slack cables are handled. The method is tested on simulated frames and on measured records of a biomimetic leg and a full-scale simplex, with reported identification errors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend physics-informed networks from forward tensegrity response to inverse prestress identification across taut-slack transitions, reporting small errors on simulated and measured record

entry.title: Rechecking Elliptic++, a Bitcoin Fraud Dataset, Without Future Data Leaks
entry.summary: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Elliptic++ is a widely used benchmark dataset for Bitcoin forensic analysis, but its split does not respect time order, letting future information leak into training. The authors recover the exact definitions of its 55 address-level features by linking to public ledger data, then recompute them using a time-based split by each address's first appearance. With leakage removed, the random forest's F1 score on the illicit class drops from 0.846 to 0.291, and it no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify temporal leakage in Elliptic++, reconstruct feature definitions via public ledger linkage, and report the illicit-class F1 for random forest dropping from 0.846 to 0.291.

entry.title: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable AI Agent for Blind 3-D MRI Artifact Correction
entry.summary: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable Agent for Blind Restoration of Multi-Artifact 3-D MRI arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents Dx-Rx, an agent that uses a multimodal large language model to restore whole 3-D brain MRI volumes without knowing which artifacts are present. It first measures suspected artifacts such as noise, spikes, ghosting, bias field and motion with diagnostic tools, then applies repair tools and checks each result. It ends with a radiology-style report explaining its diagnoses and repairs. On 148 simulated T1-weighted volumes, the best model removed a mean 64.5% of artifact error, close to the 64.6% achieved when the true artifacts were supplied. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a measure-then-repair MLLM agent restoring whole 3-D MRI volumes, reporting 64.5% artifact error removal across 148 simulated T1 volumes.

entry.title: Does an AI crowdfunding advisor favor founders by gender or ethnicity? An algorithm audit of LLM choices
entry.summary: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines whether large language model assistants that advise backers on crowdfunding campaigns favor founders based on gender or ethnicity signals. In a pre-specified choice experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with randomized quality signals and founder names, yielding 40,248 responses. By default founder names had negligible effects, but when backers wanted to support underrepresented creators, models favored Black-signaled and female-signaled founders. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that LLM assistants favor Black and female founders only when backers seek to support underrepresented creators, across seven models and about 40,248 controlled choices.

entry.title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
entry.summary: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines whether the stock-return predictability of large language models reading company news survives strict tests that rule out look-ahead, memorization and selection. The authors propose OLIVIA, a testing protocol, and apply it to non-generative language models that give probabilities for questions about S&P 500 news, including an open-weights model fine-tuned on 2024–2025 data and three commercial models. Results show the fine-tuned model's signal replicated on validation quarters but weakened on the blinded test period. The commercial models' readings match the overnight move to the open but not the move afterwards, indicating the news is priced before a trader can act on it. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose OLIVIA, a pre-registered protocol, and report that LLM news signals decay on a blinded test and are priced before the open.

entry.title: Why truncation is the best linear sketch for binary data
entry.summary: On the optimality of truncation among binary linear sketches arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies inference and function evaluation when a binary input vector is accessible only through a fixed number of parity measurements, called a binary linear sketch. Under a monotonicity condition, the authors show that simply keeping a subset of coordinates is optimal among all linear sketches of the same size. This yields lower bounds for any binary linear sketch. For a distributional graph connectivity problem on n vertices, linear sketches need Θ(n log n) bits for constant error, while a nonlinear protocol needs only O(log n) bits. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show truncation is optimal among binary linear sketches under monotonicity, and report a Θ(n log n) lower bound for graph connectivity versus O(log n) nonlinear protocols.

entry.title: ProteoCraft: protein design framed as a propose-then-verify search
entry.summary: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper treats protein design as a search optimization problem over combinatorial sequence space where structural evaluation is expensive. It introduces ProteoCraft, a tree-based search framework that uses approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors to propose where to explore, and no-gradient folding model inference to verify sequences. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings, the authors report improved design quality and high-confidence yield, and an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a tree-based search using diffusion-predictor gradients as proposal policies, evaluated across fourteen design settings and with prospective experiments.

entry.title: Forget What Comes Next: a statistical-independence method for unlearning in LLMs
entry.summary: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper introduces PINT, a machine unlearning algorithm for large language models that uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce statistical dependence between tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them. The authors relate this objective to Exact Memorization through a computable upper bound. Experiments across eight settings, with models up to 70B parameters, cover unlearning Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous biology and cybersecurity knowledge, and copyrighted books and news. PINT achieves the best forgetting-utility trade-off on average and is the only method that makes Gaussian poisons undetectable while keeping utility near the original model. ★★★★ Notable: Uses HSIC to reduce dependence between forgotten tokens and predictive representations, with a computable bound to exact memorization; the authors report experiments across eight settings up to 70B.

entry.title: AIRoA-0: Robot Manipulation Learned Entirely from Handheld Gripper Recordings
entry.summary: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper presents AIRoA-0 (A-0), a bimanual manipulation system trained on 16,151 hours of demonstrations recorded with the open-source handheld gripper YUBI, with no robot data collected at any stage. On ten evaluated tasks it reaches an average success rate of 78%, compared with 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same demonstrations. The system runs on several robot platforms that mount the YUBI gripper, and the dataset, pre-trained weights and post-training recipe are released. ★★★★ Notable: The authors train bimanual manipulation solely on handheld-gripper demonstrations, reporting 78% average success across ten tasks versus 27% for the best of four baselines.

entry.title: Unsatz: Testing whether AI can build scientific models from scratch
entry.summary: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper introduces Unsatz, a benchmark where an LLM agent must decide the model structure itself, including which variables exist, which are hidden, and how they interact. The agent buys experiments within a budget and is scored on predicting unseen conditions, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solved between 21% and 60% of tasks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a benchmark where agents build model structure themselves, reporting results across 80 systems and nine language models.

entry.title: Certifying particle indistinguishability in interferometers without tailored hardware
entry.summary: Marginal bunching for in situ certification of multiparticle indistinguishability arXiv · Oct 19, 2026The paper proposes a scalable, efficient in situ method to test whether identical bosons or fermions are indistinguishable in linear interferometer experiments. It applies to any generic linear interferometer. For particles in distinct input ports of a Haar-random unitary interferometer, the required number of runs scales polynomially with particle number, interferometer size, and inverse precision, with high probability. The method remains polynomial under uniform particle loss if the inverse single-particle survival probability is polynomially bounded. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an in situ method to certify multiparticle indistinguishability in linear interferometers, exploiting quantum parallelism and bunching/anti-bunching tendencies. The authors prove that computing the optimal value of this problem, including its Lagrangian relaxation, is NP-hard. entry.title: Do LLMs Learn from Rewards in Context? Rethinking Reward's Role in In-Context RL
entry.summary: Imitation Dominates Reinforcement: Direct In-Context RL Is Closer to ICL Than RL arXiv · Oct 8, 2026This paper tests whether LLM agents truly perform reinforcement learning at inference time by conditioning only on raw trajectory-reward pairs in context. Controlled experiments on four benchmarks and six models show that flipping, randomizing, or removing rewards barely changes the improvement curve, while shuffled or corrupted trajectories work as well as real ones. The authors conclude that direct in-context RL is better understood as a special case of in-context learning, suggesting that input distribution and demonstrations may matter more than reward shaping for agent memory design. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report controlled experiments on four benchmarks and six models finding that reward has little effect in in-context RL, and trajectory semantics matter little either, mirroring in-context

entry.title: Provably recovering secrets from integer quotients: improved bounds for nonlinear hidden number problems
entry.summary: Provable Recovery from Integer Quotients: Improved Bounds for Nonlinear Hidden Number Problems IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies the hidden number problem, which asks whether a secret can be recovered from partial information linked to it by known algebraic relations. For modulus a prime p, the authors extend provable recovery ranges for three nonlinear variants: modular inversion, elliptic-curve, and hidden-multiplier versions, tolerating a larger fraction of unrevealed lower bits. For random inputs, the algorithms run in expected time polynomial in log p and uniquely recover the secret with probability 1-o(1) as p grows. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend provable recovery ranges for three nonlinear hidden number problems, improving tolerable unrevealed bit fractions and giving polynomial expected-time algorithms.

entry.title: Maximum purity of absolutely separable and PPT quantum states in qutrit-qudit systems
entry.summary: Maximum purity of absolutely separable and absolutely PPT states in qutrit--qudit systems arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies bipartite quantum states in qutrit-qudit systems C^3⊗C^n with n≥3. It determines the maximum purity of absolutely separable states and absolutely PPT states, showing both classes share the same maximum. The authors also bound the minimum partial-transpose eigenvalue reachable by global unitary transformations in terms of purity and characterize the states attaining this bound. entry.summary: Binary Quantum Hypothesis Testing with a Rejection Option: The Exact Error-Exponent Trade-off arXiv · Oct 31, 2026The paper studies binary quantum hypothesis testing on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, where the test may reject, and the rejection probabilities under both hypotheses must vanish exponentially. entry.summary: MDS Algebraic Geometry Codes of Square-Root Length on Hyperelliptic Curves arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper constructs maximum distance separable (MDS) algebraic geometry codes over F_q for fixed genus g≥2 and any rate 0<ρ<1, for all sufficiently large odd squares q. The code length is about √q+1 plus O_g(q^{1/4}), with parameters [n,⌊ρn⌋,n-⌊ρn⌋+1]_q. The codes use full Riemann–Roch spaces on genus-g hyperelliptic curves. For large q they are not monomially equivalent to generalized Reed–Solomon (GRS) codes. ★★★★ Notable: For fixed genus g≥2 and 0<ρ<1, the authors construct MDS algebraic geometry codes of length about √q on hyperelliptic curves for large odd squares q, reporting they are not monomially equivalent to GR

entry.title: Do Fake Citations Count as Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study
entry.summary: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper examines whether language models that have undergone post-training fabricate citations because they are rewarded for appearing scholarly. Across 900 questions in US federal case law, computational science, and medical literature, tested on twelve open-weights checkpoints and refit on fifteen, asking only for citations sharply increased fabrication in post-trained models but not base models. A length-matched control indicates the effect is specific to citations rather than verbosity. entry.title: Optimal conversion from zero-concentrated to Gaussian differential privacy
entry.summary: Optimal Conversion from Zero-Concentrated to Gaussian Differential Privacy arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper examines the conversion between two privacy accounting frameworks, Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) and zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP). It shows that every ρ-zCDP mechanism satisfies μ_zCDP(ρ)-GDP and gives this optimal reverse conversion. Simplified bounds with sharp constants show the two frameworks are equivalent up to constants. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give the optimal reverse conversion from zCDP to GDP, showing every ρ-zCDP mechanism satisfies μ_zCDP(ρ)-GDP, and report simplified sharp bounds √(πρ) ≤ μ_zCDP(ρ) ≤ √(8ρ) that clarify the

entry.title: Same outputs, different scores: auditing the unchecked scoring rules of multimodal AI benchmarks
entry.summary: Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper reproduces the official scoring programs of eight peer-reviewed multiple-choice benchmarks for multimodal large language models, using five open vision-language models that run on a single 16 GB GPU. It introduces a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge procedure to recover what each model actually answered. The scoring rule alone shifts accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, but makes no difference when models output clean option letters. The authors argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two scoring rules. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit scoring rules of eight multimodal benchmarks, reproducing official scorers on five VLMs with human-plus-LLM adjudication, reporting up to 22-point accuracy swings on identical output

entry.title: Using a Vision-Language Model as a Judge for Person Re-Identification
entry.summary: VLM-as-a-Judge for Person Re-Identification arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper uses a general-purpose vision-language model, applied zero-shot, to rerank short candidate lists in cloth-changing person re-identification. On the four CHIRLA scenarios it raises rank-1 accuracy in every scenario, averaging 12.9 points above the best expert model. To cut cost, the VLM is called only when the two expert models disagree at rank 1, which removes 40% of calls without a significant rank-1 drop. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that zero-shot VLM reranking improves rank-1 on all four CHIRLA scenarios, averaging 12.9 points over the best expert, with a disagreement-based gate cutting VLM calls by 40 percent

entry.title: Agent memory as rate-limited filtering: explicit state beats long context past a reader-dependent length
entry.summary: Agent Memory as Rate-Limited Filtering: Explicit State Outlasts Long Context Beyond a Reader-Dependent Horizon arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The summary in this language did not pass the date and amount checks, so it is withheld. Check the original. ★★★★ Notable: The authors model agent memory as rate-limited recursive filtering, deriving a capacity-dependent forgetting horizon and a tight error bound, and report a reader-dependent crossover with long context.

entry.title: Lee-Yang theorems for q-deformed oscillators and doubly-scaled SYK
entry.summary: Lee-Yang theorems for q-deformed oscillators and doubly-scaled SYK arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper proves that the vacuum partition function of the q-deformed oscillator has all its zeros on the imaginary axis (the Lee-Yang property) for every q in [-1,1), confirming conjectures by Okuyama from 2023. Using the link between q-deformed oscillators and the doubly-scaled SYK Hamiltonian, the authors show that the annealed SYK partition function has the same property in the thermodynamic limit. They conclude that the quenched SYK partition function has a zero-free strip of constant width with high probability. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the q-deformed oscillator partition function has Lee-Yang zeros and extend this to doubly-scaled SYK.

entry.title: Lossless propagation bounds for long-range fermionic interactions
entry.summary: Lossless propagation bounds for long-range fermionic interactions arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper proves propagation estimates for extensive fermionic many-body interactions with polynomial time growth, no loss of spatial decay, and an optimal threshold for the polynomial spatial exponent. The authors construct local representatives of evolved interactions on metric spaces with polynomial volume growth. The threshold a > d_vol is shown to be optimal in general. The results yield dynamical estimates for perturbation theory with extensive perturbations. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give lossless propagation bounds for fermionic interactions with polynomial growth and prove the threshold a>d_vol is optimal, with applications to gap stability and adiabatic theory.

entry.title: Faster thermalization of 1D noncommuting Hamiltonians using system-bath interactions with linearly many ancillas
entry.summary: Efficient thermalization of one-dimensional noncommuting Hamiltonians via system-bath interactions with Theta(n) ancilla qubits arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper proves rapid convergence of a system-bath algorithm that prepares Gibbs states of one-dimensional noncommuting Hamiltonians at any fixed positive temperature. For a chain of n qudits, it reaches trace-norm error ε in expected total evolution time Õ(n/ε). This improves the previously proved Õ(n^6/ε) bound for single-ancilla samplers, up to logarithmic factors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the bound for single-ancilla system-bath Gibbs samplers from O(n^6) to linear system-size dependence, with theoretical analysis.

entry.title: Learning stabilizer structure under global depolarizing noise with polynomial copies
entry.summary: Stabilizer Learning under Global Depolarizing Noise with Polynomial Copies and 2^t Time arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies how to learn the stabilizer structure of an unknown pure n-qubit state observed through global depolarizing noise of unknown strength, using destructive two-copy Bell measurements. It gives a learner that uses polynomially many copies and 2^t times polynomial classical time, for any fixed noise bound below one. This answers an open question from Tang and Steckmann by exceeding their earlier noise threshold of about 0.16. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the noise threshold from about 0.16 to any fixed global depolarizing bound below one, with polynomial copies and 2^t time.

entry.title: Controlling a macroscopic free mass via continuous quantum measurement
entry.summary: Taming a macroscopic free mass through continuous quantum measurement arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper realizes a suspended 1-milligram rotor operating in the free-particle regime with strong environmental isolation. The researchers directly resolve thermal fluctuations in its motion, with a damping rate of only 7 nHz. Through continuous quantum measurement, they localize the otherwise unconfined motion, obtaining conditional states with entropic temperatures as low as 140 nK. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report controlling a 1-milligram suspended rotor in the free-particle regime via continuous quantum measurement, reaching 140 nK and applying it to tests of quantum gravity.

entry.title: Correlated catalysis eliminates the strong converse in entanglement distillation
entry.summary: Correlated Catalysis Removes the Strong Converse for Entanglement Distillation arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies entanglement distillation, which converts noisy shared quantum states into maximally entangled pairs using local operations and classical communication. It shows that correlated catalysis removes the strong converse for every distillable bipartite state. At any target rate above the distillable entanglement E_D, the optimal asymptotic fidelity equals E_D/R. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that correlated catalysis removes the strong converse, giving optimal fidelity E_D/R above the distillation rate.

entry.title: Second-order mean force Gibbs state of fermionic open systems: a paper deriving the equilibrium state of fermionic systems coupled to a reservoir, checked against exact numerics.
entry.summary: Second-order mean force Gibbs state of fermionic open systems arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper derives the grand canonical mean force Gibbs (MFG) state for a generic fermionic system coupled to a thermal reservoir at arbitrary chemical potential, to second order in the coupling. It uses the mode reduced state to make the fermionic MFG state well defined and splits the correction to the bare Gibbs state into particle and hole channels. The results are applied to the resonant level model, two modes sharing a reservoir, and the single impurity Anderson model, and checked against numerically exact and real-time dynamical calculations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive a second-order grand canonical mean force Gibbs state for fermionic systems and compare it with numerically exact and real-time results.

entry.title: unitaryQIP = unitaryPSPACE: equality of two unitary synthesis complexity classes
entry.summary: unitaryQIP = unitaryPSPACE arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies the computational cost of applying a target unitary to an unknown quantum state. It proves that the unitary complexity classes unitaryQIP and unitaryPSPACE are equal, an analogue of the earlier QIP=PSPACE and stateQIP=statePSPACE results. The authors also show the protocol can be parallelized to constant rounds when the verifier receives polynomially many input copies, and identify a complexity-theoretic barrier to proving the existence of EFI pairs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend QIP=PSPACE to unitary synthesis, proving unitaryQIP=unitaryPSPACE via an acceptance rigidity lemma and a PSPACE-oracle synthesis construction.

entry.title: Modelling NV⁻ spin-echo decoherence in nitrogen-rich diamond with a dynamical mean field
entry.summary: Dynamical-mean-field cluster-correlation expansion of NV⁻ spin-echo decoherence in a realistic substitutional-nitrogen bath arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies the Hahn-echo coherence time T₂ of NV⁻ centres in nitrogen-rich diamond. The authors replace the frozen mean field of surrounding P1 centres with a dynamical one, where pairs of P1 centres flip-flop while conserving total Sz, with rates from the dipolar Hamiltonian via kinetic Monte Carlo. At 30 mT this lowers T₂·[N] from 264 to 188 μs ppm, closer to experiment, without dark spins. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a dynamical mean field for CCE that replaces the frozen field, reporting parameter-free agreement with experiment at 10 and 30 mT and a remaining low-field discrepancy.

entry.title: Barycentric programming: classical programs for universal quantum processors
entry.summary: Barycentric programming: Classical realization of programs for universal quantum processors arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper introduces barycentric programming, which stores the label of a unitary chosen randomly from a finite set, with probabilities set so that first-order approximation errors cancel in the averaged channel. As a result, the diamond-distance error scales quadratically with the discretization spacing. For ν-parameter unitary families forming a compact smooth manifold without boundary, the method achieves error ε using (ν/2)log₂(1/ε)+O(1) classical bits. The authors also prove a matching lower bound for arbitrary quantum programs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce barycentric programming, using randomized classical labels to cancel first-order errors and match the optimal leading-order program size, with a matching lower bound.

entry.title: Quantum Temporal Marginal Problem: whether partial multi-time experiments can come from one quantum process
entry.summary: Quantum Temporal Marginal Problem arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper asks whether partial measurement results from a quantum process at selected times can come from one common underlying process. The authors formulate this process tensor marginal problem as a semidefinite feasibility test. They show that agreement on overlapping times is not sufficient, and quantify incompatibility by the mixing needed to restore compatibility. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formulate a process tensor marginal problem as an SDP, report that local consistency is insufficient, and show incompatibility equals a discrimination advantage.

entry.title: Detection times are not local observables in quantum field theory
entry.summary: Detection times are not local observables in quantum field theory arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper shows that, under natural covariance and consistency requirements, observables describing detection times cannot be algebraically localized in any bounded spacetime region, even when the records themselves are localized. This challenges equating algebraic localization with the physical localization of measurements. The authors further argue that microcausality alone does not establish non-signalling for measurements in quantum field theory. ★★★★ Notable: The authors argue that detection-time observables cannot be algebraically localized in bounded regions, challenging the usual identification with physical localization of measurements.

entry.title: Phase-conjugate twin-wave coherent reception over 100 km of fiber using injection locking
entry.summary: Experimental demonstration of phase-conjugated twin-wave coherent reception over 100 km with injection locking assisted phase stabilization arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper experimentally demonstrates a coherent receiver that recovers 200-MBaud signals with modulation formats up to 256-QAM after 100 km of optical fiber. Optical injection locking regenerates the local oscillator from a reference sent through the link, and pilot-assisted optical feedback stabilizes the signal-to-local-oscillator phase so that phase-conjugated twin waves combine at one balanced photodetector. The reported signal-to-noise ratio exceeds the ideal single-mode homodyne standard quantum limit benchmark and conventional heterodyne results by about 3 dB and 6 dB, respectively. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report injection-locked phase-conjugated twin-wave reception over 100 km, with measured SNR above the single-mode SQL benchmark.

entry.title: Recovering quantum information from black-hole radiation beyond the mean emission yield
entry.summary: Quantum Recovery from Black-Hole Radiation Beyond the Emission Yield arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper asks how much information an outside observer can recover from radiation escaping a black hole. At a fixed mean radiation yield, it establishes a sharp recovery limit for single-excitation channels and realizes the qubit limit with an autonomous quantum-memory emitter. Unequal transmissions balance retained coherence against information in failed collection events. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish a recovery frontier at fixed mean radiation yield for single-excitation channels and realize its qubit limit with a quantum-memory emitter.

entry.title: From ghost SICs to SIC-POVMs: a Galois reduction of Zauner's conjecture
entry.summary: From Ghost SICs to SIC-POVMs: A Galois Reduction of Zauner's Conjecture arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper studies the existence of symmetric informationally complete POVMs (SIC-POVMs) in quantum information. The authors compute the isolated points of the complexified SIC variety for dimensions 4, 5 and 6, finding that exactly half are SICs. They show that passing from ghost SICs to genuine SICs is purely arithmetic and give a criterion based on a place law over a real quadratic field. Zauner's conjecture remains unproven in this work. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce ghost-to-SIC passage to arithmetic via a Galois place law, reporting computations for d=4,5,6 and proofs for several dimensions, with the Stark part unproved.

entry.title: Near-optimal learning of quantum many-body Hamiltonians from Gibbs and metastable thermal states
entry.summary: Near-Optimal Learning of Quantum Many-Body Systems from Gibbs and Thermal Metastable States via the Stationarity Test arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies learning a finite-range quantum Hamiltonian on an n-qubit lattice from copies of its Gibbs states at known inverse temperature β, or from its thermal metastable states. The proposed algorithm reduces the exponential dependence on β from e^{poly(β)} to e^{O(β)}, nearly optimal in the exponent. It builds on a stationarity-test framework and a temperature-independent frequency filter. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the temperature exponent in Hamiltonian learning sample complexity from poly(β) to linear in β, proving a Fisher-information coercivity bound.

entry.title: A paper on maximum purity, absolute separability, and spectral volumes of absolutely PPT quantum states
entry.summary: Purity maxima, absolute separability, and spectral volumes of absolutely PPT states arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT) states and absolutely separable states in m⊗n quantum systems. Under specified dimension conditions, it determines their exact maximum purity and the unique maximizing ordered spectrum. These results disprove both cases of a maximum purity conjecture proposed by Ahiable, Kothakonda, and Winter. The paper also computes the purity maximum for completely absolutely separable states and the asymptotic order of the relative volumes of these sets under the uniform spectral measure. ★★★★ Notable: The authors determine exact maximum purity and unique maximizing spectra for APPT and absolutely separable states, disproving a conjecture with explicit boundary spectra in quantum entanglement theory

entry.title: Boson sampling is weak against photon loss
entry.summary: Boson sampling is fragile to loss arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper asks whether boson sampling experiments remain computationally hard when photons are lost. It shows that even a small, fixed, nonzero uniform loss rate lets a classical computer sample the output distribution efficiently on average. The method exploits the fact that loss suppresses many-photon correlations, so low correlation orders suffice for approximation. The authors conclude that a large photon count alone does not guarantee computational hardness. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that any fixed nonzero uniform photon loss allows average-case efficient classical sampling of boson sampling, with polynomial-time samplers for Fock and Gaussian variants.

entry.title: Exponentially Suppressed Bit-Flip Errors in Dissipative Cat Qubits
entry.summary: Exponential suppression of bit-flip errors in dissipative cat qubits arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies a dissipative cat qubit subject to single-photon loss, described by the infinite-dimensional Lindblad generator L_ε=D[a²−α²]+εD[a]. For sufficiently large α and sufficiently small ε, it identifies a two-dimensional spectral subspace near zero. The authors establish an upper bound on the slow decay rate that decreases exponentially with α², uniformly in ε, proving exponential suppression of bit-flip errors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove an exponentially small upper bound on the bit-flip decay rate in a dissipative cat qubit, uniform in the loss rate, a result relevant to quantum error correction.

entry.title: Density functionals for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian
entry.summary: Density functionals for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper builds a density-functional theory for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian of nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics, following Lieb's convex-analytic approach. It uses the electron density and a combined current density as basic variables and proves representability results for these density-current pairs. The authors also analyze the mixed-state and pure-state functionals, the zero-coupling limit, and the long-wavelength dipole limit. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend Lieb's convex-analytic density-functional framework to the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian, proving representability, attainment of the infimum, zero-coupling recovery of Vignale-Rasolt, an

entry.title: Qubit links across a metamaterial, with less stray entanglement
entry.summary: All-to-All Connectivity in Superconducting Qubits via Metamaterial-Mediated Interactions arXiv · Nov 1, 2026This paper proposes encoding superconducting qubits as dual-rail or spin-locked transmons coupled all-to-all through a metamaterial waveguide. The encoding suppresses spurious entanglement from shared-mode architectures. A simulation of two dual-rail transmons gives a gate infidelity of 1.4×10⁻³ over 152 ns, dominated by photon loss. The paper also bounds the array size under photon loss and mode crowding. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose encoded transmons in a metamaterial waveguide for all-to-all coupling; simulations of two dual-rail qubits report 1.4e-3 gate infidelity at 152 ns.

entry.title: Limits on estimating several quantum parameters at once, for general and adaptive sensing strategies
entry.summary: Multiparameter quantum metrology for general and adaptive strategies arXiv · Nov 1, 2026The paper develops a conic-programming framework for estimating several parameters of a quantum process under different classes of sensing strategies. For N uses of an identical channel, it proves an exact 1/N scaling for an RLD-based positive-cone lower bound, even with indefinite causal order. For fixed-order adaptive strategies, each process-side conic bound matches the state-estimation bound optimized over sensor combs. A noisy three-parameter field-sensing model illustrates the framework. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a conic-programming framework for multiparameter quantum process estimation, prove an exact 1/N RLD positive-cone bound including indefinite causal order, and show equality with se

entry.title: Light cones of information spread in long-range bosonic quantum systems
entry.summary: Lieb-Robinson Light Cones in Long-Range Bosonic Systems arXiv · Oct 31, 2026The paper studies Lieb-Robinson bounds, which limit how fast information can spread in quantum many-body systems, for interacting bosons with long-range interactions. It derives upper and lower bounds whose light-cone exponents depend on the decay exponent α and the bosonic interaction order p. For p≥4 and 2d<α≤2d+1, the upper and lower exponents coincide, determining the optimal leading light-cone power. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive matching-exponent upper and lower light-cone bounds for long-range unbounded bosonic systems, governed by decay exponent and interaction order.

entry.title: Information loss from random measurements in quantum metrology, showing how randomly chosen measurement bases keep or lose sensing information.
entry.summary: The exact information cost of randomized measurements in quantum metrology arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper examines how much quantum Fisher information (QFI) randomized measurements retain in quantum sensing. It shows that 2-designs, such as complete mutually unbiased bases and SIC measurements, can lose a fixed fraction of QFI in the worst case, while 3-designs retain a constant fraction for every pure state. It attributes the loss to the geometry of aligned blind spots, and reports that independent Haar-random bases and random Clifford measurements keep a fixed fraction of QFI. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show 2-designs need not retain quantum Fisher information, give exact retention fractions for MUBs and SICs, explain the loss via blind-spot geometry, and analyze Haar and Clifford random

entry.title: Quantum channel tomography: optimal query bounds near the boundary
entry.summary: Quantum channel tomography: optimal bounds in the near-boundary regime arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies quantum channel tomography, which learns the full description of an unknown quantum channel from black-box queries. It resolves the open query complexity in the near-boundary regime, where the dilation rate is slightly above 1, and gives tight bounds for both diamond norm and Choi trace norm error. The results show that the transition from Heisenberg to classical scaling occurs abruptly for diamond norm error but gradually for Choi trace norm error. ★★★★ Notable: The authors close the near-boundary gap, reporting matching tight bounds for diamond and Choi trace norm tomography, revealing two distinct Heisenberg-to-classical transitions.

entry.title: Strategist: Evolving AI Reasoning Strategies with Agents
entry.summary: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper introduces Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Strategies are stored as reusable executable code blueprints in a shared library, retrieved for new tasks, tested on a small development set, and revised based on results. Across 30 benchmarks, it beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs. 74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. ★★★★ Notable: Meta-agent evolves reusable inference-strategy blueprints across tasks; authors report beating the strongest baseline on 24 of 30 benchmarks at 39% lower cost.

entry.title: Scaling Theory for Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Stage Overfitting and Ensembling
entry.summary: A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly affect generalization when training data is fixed. In language model experiments on FineWeb, averaging logits reduces late-training performance decline and delays the optimal stopping point. The authors derive a dynamical mean-field theory for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles and use it to give compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model size. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors derive a DMFT theory for multi-epoch SGD with ensembling and compute-allocation laws, reporting FineWeb language-model experiments where ensembles outperform wider or deeper single models.

entry.title: NitiBench+: A Time-Aware Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains
entry.summary: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper introduces NitiBench+, a Thai legal question answering benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it provides both the text in force on the decision date and the current text. Evaluating 13 open-weight models, the authors find that using the current text of amended law or missing repealed law lowers scores, while a public leaderboard of 26 models shows that today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law. ★★★★ Notable: The authors evaluate Thai legal QA on text in force at decision date, reporting score drops across 1,670 items and 13 open models.

entry.title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
entry.summary: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper measures how attacker-controlled tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data in the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can manipulate agentic AI systems. The authors propose a 25-class root-cause taxonomy and build the open-source tool mcpvenom to run a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios. The overall attack success rate is 22.9%, and 12.1% of vulnerable cells verifiably exfiltrate a secret. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real execution, a 25-class taxonomy, and a 9,720-cell matrix across 12 frameworks and 18 models.

entry.title: CoLa3D: Composable Latent 3D Scene Decomposition
entry.summary: CoLa3D: Composable Latent 3D Decomposition arXiv · Nov 3, 2026CoLa3D is a model that takes a single whole-scene latent, derived from one image or an existing scene mesh, and outputs a set of object meshes with consistent spatial layout that can be reassembled into a coherent scene. It uses a lightweight, query-based transformer that accepts 2D masks, 3D points, or learnable queries. On synthetic and real-world datasets it reports state-of-the-art performance on composable 3D scene decomposition, running 2 times faster than SAM 3D with less than 1% of its training data. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report decomposing objects directly within a shared scene latent, beating SAM 3D on synthetic and real data while running twice as fast.

entry.title: Attacks That Stop Messages Reaching Nodes in P2P Gossip Networks
entry.summary: Attacking P2P Networks: Liveness Attacks on the GossipSub and DOG Gossip Protocols arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how two peer-to-peer gossip protocols, GossipSub (used by Ethereum) and DOG (designed for CometBFT), hold up against attackers who only aim to keep honest nodes from receiving fresh messages. For GossipSub, the authors show that a few geographically distributed nodes with a latency advantage can capture the peer-scoring metric for first message deliveries and separate a constant fraction of nodes from the honest mesh. For DOG, they show a single physical node can disable all forwarding routes, leaving only direct publisher-to-neighbor delivery, and they verify this attack in a simulated network. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report liveness attacks exploiting GossipSub's First Message Deliveries scoring and DOG's route filtering, verified in simulation, with cost and mitigation analysis.

entry.title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation
entry.summary: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper weakens the three equivalent descriptions of convexity with one distortion parameter γ in (0,1], producing nested function classes that are convex at γ=1. The authors show these classes have convex effective domains, with local minimizers that are global and local Lipschitz continuity on the relative interior. Assuming NP≠RP, no polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves sublinear α-regret online for fixed γ in (0,1), so γ is the exact online coefficient while the offline coefficient is one. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a distortion parameter γ weakening convexity, prove nested classes, and report an exact offline-online separation with a hardness lower bound.

entry.title: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users at Different Skill Levels
entry.summary: Playing Dumb: How a Chess Transformer Simulates Users Across Skill Levels arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies Maia-2, a chess transformer that predicts human moves based on player skill. Using probes, the authors show that its internal encoding of 172 chess concepts stays nearly constant across skill levels. Fine-tuning only the final output layer raised best-move accuracy in the lowest skill band from 14.4% to 82.8%. The results suggest weaker play reflects how retained knowledge is used rather than a lack of knowledge. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate knowledge encoding from knowledge use in Maia-2, reporting probes, output-layer fine-tuning, and sparse autoencoder steering, with lowest-skill best-move accuracy rising from 14.4

entry.title: IAMRAGBENCH: Testing whether AI-generated AWS IAM policies grant excess access under poisoned retrieval
entry.summary: IAMRAGBENCH: Benchmarking Authorization Expansions in LLM-Generated AWS IAM Policies under RAG Poisoning arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper introduces IAMRAGBENCH, a 60-case benchmark that tests whether large language models using retrieval-augmented generation produce AWS IAM policies granting more access than the task allows when attacker-controlled documents are in the context. Across several model endpoints, poisoned context led to many policies that exceed the trusted authorization envelope, and the authors also assess how well AWS CheckNoNewAccess detects these changes. The authors conclude that IAM copilots should be treated as untrusted proposal generators whose outputs need independent authorization checks before deployment. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a benchmark quantifying RAG-poisoning-induced IAM authorization expansion and propose pre-deployment independent authorization checks.

entry.title: DeliverBench: Testing whether AI agents can deliver full multi-stage professional projects
entry.summary: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper introduces DeliverBench, a benchmark that tests whether AI agents can take a professional project from initial brief to final delivery. It contains 11 projects in areas such as financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting, built by 13 domain experts from real materials and divided into 150 subtasks with 2 to 15 rounds of new materials and client feedback. Agents inherit their own earlier errors, and experts score each checkpoint and the final package. The best of seven model-harness systems scored 65.0 out of 100 on final delivery and passed 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. The authors conclude that task-level ability does not simply add up to successful delivery, which also requires keeping the work coherent as it evolves. ★★★★ Notable: The authors evaluate multi-stage professional project delivery with expert rubrics, reporting the best system scores 65.0 out of 100 on final delivery.

entry.title: At What Cost? Inefficiency in First-Price Procurement Auctions
entry.summary: At What Cost? (In)efficiency in First-Price Procurement Auctions arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the efficiency of Bayes-Nash equilibria in first-price procurement auctions, measured by the Price of Anarchy, which compares equilibrium expected social cost to the optimal minimum. It shows that the standard format has no bounded efficiency guarantee. It then introduces a phantom bidder mechanism to restore a finite bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show unbounded PoA for standard first-price procurement, derive a tight bound, and propose phantom-bidder mechanisms with matching lower bounds.

entry.title: SIMPLE Law: A Four-Parameter Model for Predicting LLM Inference Energy
entry.summary: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper derives closed-form expressions for the computation and memory-access costs of LLM inference from architectural hyperparameters and proposes SIMPLE, a four-parameter energy model that separates prefill from decode. Tested on 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it reaches R² of 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE without per-model calibration. The paper also analyzes how input length, grouped-query attention, reasoning token budgets, and agentic serving with prefix caching affect energy use. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive closed-form energy models from architecture hyperparameters, proposing a four-parameter law reporting R2 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE across 13 LLMs, relevant to inference energy planning.

entry.title: Calibrated Multiaccuracy: Sample Complexity of Deterministic and Randomized Predictors
entry.summary: Calibrated Multiaccuracy: Deterministic and Randomized Sample Complexity arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies calibrated multiaccuracy, where a predictor is globally calibrated and multiaccurate with respect to a bounded test family G, meaning its residuals are uncorrelated with every test function. The authors determine its sample complexity, which differs from that of multicalibration, and give an upper bound achieved by a randomized predictor. For deterministic predictors they establish a tight rate, revealing a genuine sample-complexity separation between the two. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish tight sample complexity for calibrated multiaccuracy, separating it from multicalibration and showing a deterministic versus randomized predictor gap.

entry.title: Top-k Retrieval Leaves Memory Value Undetermined
entry.summary: Top-k Retrieval Leaves Memory Value Undetermined arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper asks which memory values an agent can infer from its retrieval log alone. It proves that under top-k retrieval, no memory value is determined however many episodes are logged. The proposed LEDGER method estimates only the determined Shapley values, with confidence intervals, and raises the fraction of determined memories on pooled HotpotQA from 0.001 to 0.797. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove top-k retrieval logs leave memory values undetermined and propose LEDGER, reporting a large rise in determined memories on HotpotQA.

entry.title: Predicting RLHF policy responses to reward-model edits before training
entry.summary: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies how an RLHF policy changes when its reward model is edited. The authors propose forecasting the policy's response before training, using samples from the current policy and the scores of the old and new reward models. In 54 controlled RL runs, the covariance-based forecast predicts the direction of most feature changes and holds under GRPO and real reward-model upgrades. ★★★★ Notable: The authors predict policy responses to reward-model edits before training via within-prompt covariance, reporting pre-registered validation across 54 RL runs and real upgrades.

entry.title: CERBO: A method for training gradient-boosted trees that offers certified recourse at a requested rate
entry.summary: CERBO: Certified Recourse at a Requested Rate for Gradient-Boosted Trees arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper presents CERBO, a method for training gradient-boosted decision trees so that people receiving an adverse decision can reverse it with an affordable change. Given a requested recourse rate, the method adjusts its weight after each tree until the certified rate meets the target, and a calibration step extends the guarantee to new individuals. In the authors' experiments, CERBO raised recourse rates at equal accuracy and improved the accuracy-recourse frontier across the tested settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a GBDT training method targeting a requested recourse rate with certified actions, reporting gains over RABIT on FICO, Bail, and six datasets.

entry.title: Pricing LLM services from a cold start under two-sided learning
entry.summary: Cold-Start Pricing of LLM Services under Two-Sided Learning arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies how providers of online large language model services can set prices when they lack historical data, while users' willingness to pay changes with repeated use. It models the problem as two-sided learning, where the user learns from private experience and the provider adjusts prices using only purchase decisions. The authors derive matching minimax regret bounds across two serving-cost regimes and propose corresponding algorithms. Simulations confirm the predicted regret scaling and show the algorithms outperform standard online learning baselines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formulate LLM pricing cold start as two-sided learning, derive matching minimax regret bounds with a cost-dependent phase transition, and report simulations supporting the predicted scalin

entry.title: Written Once, Read Differently: How Language Models' Own Answers Steer Later Ones
entry.summary: Written Once, Read Differently How Language Models Own Answers Steer Their Next Ones arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The study examines 22 open-weight language models (0.5B to 72B parameters) by fixing each model's answer to a yes/no question and measuring how it shifts the answer to a second question about the same entity, across 3,600 question pairs about 120 entities. Each answer writes a commitment direction into the residual stream, and the similarity of two questions' directions predicts how strongly their answers are coupled. How this direction is read, however, varies with model scale, instruction tuning and system prompt, and in one model the sign of the effect reverses. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that a model's own earlier answer writes a commitment direction shaping later answers, tested across 22 models and 3,600 question pairs.

entry.title: Autonomous agent that tunes MSA construction to improve protein complex structure prediction
entry.summary: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper studies how the depth and cross-chain pairing of multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) affect AlphaFold 3's prediction of protein complex structures, finding the best strategy depends on the target. The authors introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black box, forming biological hypotheses and iteratively reorganizing MSAs and pairing choices, including deliberate non-pairing, using label-free confidence signals. Across 1,015 protein-protein interfaces from three benchmarks, the agent improves overall DockQ over the default pipeline and fixed recipes while using on average 60% fewer MSA sequences. The largest gains occur for inter-species heteromers, with mean DockQ rising from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat MSA design as target-specific and adapt it at test time with an autonomous agent; they report DockQ gains over AF3's default on 1,015 interfaces across three benchmarks.

entry.title: ViAdminShift: A Vietnamese benchmark testing whether language models update knowledge after the 2025 administrative reform
entry.summary: ViAdminShift: A Vietnamese Benchmark for Event-Level Knowledge Updates Built from the 2025 Administrative Reform arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper presents ViAdminShift, a Vietnamese benchmark built around the July 1, 2025 administrative reorganization that cut Vietnam's provinces and communes. It includes 7,995 benchmark items and 2,281 retrieval passages. The authors test 67 models and find that many still give old provinces for old addresses, with the answer changing when a date is given in the prompt. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build an event-level benchmark from Vietnam's 2025 administrative reform and report probing results on 67 models, including outdated-answer rates.

entry.title: Reed-Muller codes are optimal linear 3-query locally correctable codes
entry.summary: Reed-Muller Codes are Optimal Binary Linear 3-Query LCCs arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper proves that any linear 3-query locally correctable code with constant correction radius must have length at least 2 raised to Ω(√k). The previous best lower bound was 2 raised to Ω(√(k/log k)). The result shows that linear 3-LCCs built from Reed-Muller codes, which have length 2 raised to O(√k), are optimal up to constant factors in the exponent. The proof combines chain-derived equations with Kikuchi graphs and shows that a certain edge-coloured Kikuchi graph has a unique colour cycle. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the length lower bound for linear 3-query LCCs to 2^Ω(√k), showing Reed-Muller constructions are optimal up to constant exponent factors.

entry.title: A study of how much information privacy filters and odometers need to work well.
entry.summary: An Information Hierarchy of Privacy Filters and Odometers arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies how the information used by differential privacy filters and odometers limits their performance. It defines three information levels (spec, mechanism, and realisation) and classifies filters and odometers by the least informative level sufficient to determine their behaviour. The main results show strict and arbitrarily large performance gaps across this hierarchy, and that randomisation offers a separate resource that can also yield large utility gains. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalise a three-level information hierarchy and report arbitrarily large separations in filter and odometer performance across levels.

entry.title: DR Pixel: Deep Research Directly on Document Page Images with Vision-Language Models
entry.summary: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper introduces DR Pixel, an open-source multimodal research agent that retrieves and reasons over rendered page images instead of OCR-extracted text, across a 1.06M-page corpus. The authors also build DRPixelBench, a benchmark of scientific papers requiring reasoning over text, figures, tables, and equations. The approach outperforms OCR-based baselines even without training, and a counterfactual credit reweighting method further improves retrieval recall and accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a page-native multimodal research agent with counterfactual credit reweighting, reporting gains over OCR baselines on DRPixelBench and four other benchmarks.

entry.title: A fine-grained difficulty ladder and benchmark for how language models track changing states
entry.summary: A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper proposes a four-level hierarchy of word problems, from simple immutable variable assignment to general finite state tracking, to evaluate how well language models track state. It theoretically compares transformers with recurrent architectures such as Gated DeltaNet, and builds StateBench, a long-horizon benchmark based on these levels. Direct training experiments largely match the theoretical predictions, while pretrained models, both open and closed, do not robustly solve even soluble state tracking. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a four-level state-tracking hierarchy and benchmark, with theoretical characterizations of several architectures and direct-training and pretrained-model evaluations.

entry.title: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion
entry.summary: One Image Is Enough: Self-Generated Supervision for Personalizing Human Video Diffusion at Test Time arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper addresses pose-driven human video diffusion models, which struggle to keep a person's identity consistent when the target pose differs from the reference image. Instead of requiring multi-pose subject videos, the authors synthesize pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses with a pose-conditioned generator, select the most identity-consistent ones using a reference-only sampler, and train a per-subject low-rank adapter on them. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves over the base on every metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames. ★★★★ Notable: The authors replace real multi-pose subject video with synthesized pseudo-ground-truth frames for personalization, reporting gains on TikTok and UBC Fashion.

entry.title: Generative diffusion on long-range correlated landscapes: how the reverse process commits to data
entry.summary: Generative diffusion in long-range correlated landscapes: Speciation cascade and the foam structure of the score arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies why generative diffusion works, using the Gibbs measure of a high-dimensional Gaussian random potential with long-range correlations as an analytically tractable data model. With the exact score, the authors show that the reverse process gradually resolves the branches of pure states and commits to a single one within a speciation window. They describe the score as a foam of slab-like cells separated by shock-like boundaries, and show that the denoising error drops in stages that follow this process. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyze reverse diffusion on Gibbs measures of long-range correlated Gaussian potentials, introducing a foam structure and Larkin-type argument for O(1) energy gaps.
